segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The book of the origin of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Abraham fathered Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez fathered Hezron, and Hezron fathered Ram.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, and Obed fathered Jesse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesse fathered David the king. David fathered Solomon by Uriah’s wife.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Solomon fathered Rehoboam, Rehoboam fathered Abijah, and Abijah fathered Asaph.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat fathered Joram, and Joram fathered Uzziah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Uzziah fathered Jotham, Jotham fathered Ahaz, and Ahaz fathered Hezekiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, Manasseh fathered Amos, and Amos fathered Josiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Josiah fathered Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Zerubbabel fathered Abiud, Abiud fathered Eliakim, and Eliakim fathered Azor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Azor fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Achim, and Achim fathered Eliud.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, and Matthan fathered Jacob.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Messiah fourteen generations.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the origin of Jesus Christ was like this. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph her husband, being righteous and not wanting to disgrace her publicly, decided to divorce her quietly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he had thought this over, look, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife into your home, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: She will give birth to a son, and you are to call his name Jesus, for it is he who will save his people from their sins.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All this happened so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet would be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Look, the virgin will become pregnant and will give birth to a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which is translated “God with us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took his wife into his home,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he did not sleep with her until she had given birth to a son; and he called his name Jesus.

notes.note: The same Greek word, genesis, stands here and in verse 18, and most translations hide the link by using two different English words. The opening phrase echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, which a reader of the Septuagint would have recognised. Scholars disagree whether verse 1 is a heading for the genealogy alone, for the birth account, or for the whole Gospel; “origin” leaves that open and keeps the repetition.

Ancient Jewish genealogies normally ran through fathers only, so the naming of four women before Mary (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Uriah’s wife, Bathsheba) is deliberate. Why these four is debated: all have foreign connections, and each came into the line through an irregular or unexpected union. Either feature, or both, may prepare the reader for Mary.

The earliest manuscripts read Asaph here and Amos in verse 10, where the Old Testament names the kings Asa and Amon; later manuscripts have Asa and Amon. Whether these were accepted variant spellings of the kings’ names or an early confusion with the psalmist Asaph and the prophet Amos is disputed. The translation gives the names as the Greek text has them.

The Greek christos means “anointed” and renders the Hebrew word that gives English “Messiah”, the anointed king Israel expected. Where the word functions as a title, as here and in verse 17, this translation uses “Messiah”; where it is attached to “Jesus” as part of his name, as in verses 1 and 18, it keeps “Christ”. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

The scheme is stylised, not a complete list: comparison with the Old Testament shows that several kings are passed over between Joram and Uzziah, and the verb “fathered” can cover a more distant ancestor. It is often suggested that fourteen was chosen because the Hebrew letters of David’s name add up to that number. This is plausible but cannot be proved.

notes.traditional: betrothed; engaged; pledged to be married
notes.note: Jewish betrothal was a legally binding contract, not an engagement in the modern sense. It could be ended only by divorce or death, which is why Joseph is already called Mary’s husband and considers divorce. The couple did not yet live together; “came together” refers to the beginning of their shared life, including sexual union.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify), so the connection between these words is harder to see in English. Here the word describes a man who lives in accordance with God’s law. Whether Joseph’s reluctance to shame Mary is an expression of that righteousness or a mercy that tempers it is left open by the Greek.

notes.phrase: to take Mary your wife into your home
notes.traditional: to take Mary as your wife
notes.note: The Greek calls Mary “your wife” already, since betrothal made her so in law. The verb means to take someone along or receive them to oneself, and here refers to the second stage of marriage, when the husband brought his bride into his house. The traditional wording suggests the marriage itself had yet to be contracted.

“Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua (Yeshua), which was understood to mean “the LORD saves”. The angel’s explanation, “for it is he who will save”, depends on that meaning. The wordplay is invisible in Greek as it is in English.

The quotation is Isaiah 7:14 in its Greek form. The Greek word normally means a virgin, while the Hebrew word in Isaiah means a young woman of marriageable age without specifying virginity. Matthew cites the verse as it stood in the Greek Scriptures his readers knew.

The Greek says literally that he “was not knowing her”, a biblical idiom for sexual intercourse familiar from the Septuagint. A modern reader may not recognise the idiom, so an equivalent English euphemism is used. The Greek tense indicates continued abstention over the period.

The Greek construction states what was the case up to the birth and does not in itself say what happened afterwards. Traditions that hold Mary remained a virgin read it as silent about the later period; most Protestant interpreters take it to imply ordinary marital relations after the birth. The grammar alone does not settle the question.

candidates.reason: Extremely frequent across the New Testament; translators vary between “behold”, “look”, “see”, “suddenly” and omission, and a single policy is needed for narrative and speech.

candidates.rendering: fathered (active, of a father); was born / conceived (passive)

Used for divorce in the Synoptic divorce sayings but also for dismissing crowds and releasing prisoners; the divorce sense in particular needs one fixed rendering (not “put away” or “send away”).
